items.question:
A content manager at a non-profit advocacy organisation uses Claude to draft monthly donor newsletters. After three iterations, the current draft is factually accurate, covers all required topics, uses the correct brand tone, and has passed a bias review. The content manager is dissatisfied with one turn of phrase in the third paragraph and wants another iteration. Her manager asks her to articulate when iterative refinement should stop.

What principle BEST defines the stopping point?

options.A: Iteration should stop when the content manager is fully satisfied with every sentence in the output.
options.B: Iteration should stop when the output meets all pre-defined acceptance criteria — further refinement beyond that threshold produces diminishing returns.
options.C: Iteration should stop after a fixed maximum of three cycles regardless of output quality.
options.D: Iteration should stop when a fresh reviewer would be needed to provide objective feedback.

items.question:
An EA to an investment manager drafts quarterly client letters using Claude for a portfolio of 40 clients. Under a 90-minute deadline, one draft is identified with two issues: (1) the portfolio's year-to-date return is stated as 11.2% when it should be 11.7%, and (2) the letter's tone is warmer and more conversational than the firm's standard formal investor-communication register. Both issues are confirmed in the same review pass.

Which quality dimension should be fixed FIRST?

options.A: Tone first — regulatory standards for investor communications specify strict format compliance.
options.B: Both simultaneously — neither is acceptable, and a single edit pass can address both.
options.C: Factual accuracy first — distributing an incorrect return figure is a material misstatement with regulatory and fiduciary consequences.
options.D: Tone first — tone errors are faster to fix, preserving maximum time for the accuracy correction.

items.question:
An insurance claims handler uses Claude to extract all coverage exclusions from a 40-page homeowner policy. The policy contains 12 numbered exclusion clauses. Claude's output lists 11 exclusions. The handler needs to determine whether the extraction is complete.

What is the BEST method to verify completeness?

options.A: Ask Claude to re-run the extraction from the same document and check whether both outputs match.
options.B: Accept the output — an 11-of-12 extraction rate exceeds 90% and is sufficient for claims review.
options.C: Read the entire 40-page policy end-to-end to identify any exclusion Claude may have missed.
options.D: Search the source document for the missing item by systematically checking each policy section against the 11-item extraction list to find the gap.

items.question:
A QA lead at a 200-person logistics company implemented a rubric for reviewing Claude-generated delivery-exception reports two months ago. Two trained reviewers are now applying the rubric, but reviewer 1 passes 85% of outputs while reviewer 2 passes only 65% of the same outputs. Both reviewers completed the same training.

What is the MOST likely cause, and what is the MOST appropriate resolution?

options.A: The reviewers have drifted to different rubric interpretations; a calibration session where both review the same outputs and reconcile disagreements will realign them.
options.B: One reviewer is applying a higher standard, which should be adopted as the new official threshold.
options.C: The rubric is too strict; it should be relaxed to increase the overall pass rate.
options.D: The difference indicates one reviewer is not following the rubric and should be replaced.

items.question:
A diversity recruiter at a large telecoms company reviews a Claude-generated shortlist rationale for a senior engineering role. The document correctly identifies that all five shortlisted candidates meet the stated technical requirements. A colleague points out that the language describing male candidates uses terms like 'technically strong' and 'decisive,' while female candidates are described as 'technically competent' and 'collaborative.'

What quality dimension does the colleague's observation primarily identify?

options.A: Factual inaccuracy — the differential descriptions misrepresent the candidates' qualifications.
options.B: Bias — the language applies different evaluative framing to candidates based on gender.
options.C: Completeness — the rationale is missing standardised assessment language across all candidates.
options.D: Register mismatch — 'collaborative' is less technically formal than 'decisive.'

items.question:
A research operations coordinator at a pharma company is building a golden set to benchmark Claude's protocol-section summaries. She consults a senior researcher, who recommends including only the five most recent, cleanest protocols because they provide the clearest examples of correct summaries.

What is the PRIMARY quality risk in the senior researcher's selection approach?

options.A: Five protocols is statistically too small to support a reliable benchmark.
options.B: Recent protocols may reflect regulatory guidance changes that post-date Claude's training.
options.C: A set containing only simple, well-formed cases will not reveal performance on complex or ambiguous protocols, overstating Claude's accuracy on the full task range.
options.D: Using protocols the researcher considers 'correct' introduces subjective bias into the ground truth.

items.question:
A senior policy analyst at a public sector think-tank asks Claude to draft a briefing note that will serve two purposes: (1) an internal working-group discussion document for a team of subject-matter experts, and (2) after light editing, a public-facing executive summary for a minister's briefing pack. The same draft will be used for both purposes. She is writing acceptance criteria and realises the two uses carry different quality standards.

What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.A: Define acceptance criteria for the internal use first, then add supplementary checks specifically for the external use.
options.B: Apply the internal document's criteria, since the external version will receive separate editorial attention before distribution.
options.C: Apply identical criteria to both uses, since the document is the same draft regardless of audience.
options.D: Define criteria against the higher-stakes use (the ministerial briefing), since that sets the binding quality floor for the shared draft.

items.question: A risk manager at a mid-tier bank is designing an escalation policy for Claude outputs used in loan risk assessments. He wants the policy to be specific enough to guide reviewers without creating excessive overhead. Which TWO elements are essential components of an effective escalation policy? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Specific, observable quality signals that trigger escalation, such as unverifiable claims or internal contradictions.
options.B: A requirement that Claude provide a confidence percentage for each risk assessment output.
options.C: Named escalation recipients with defined response-time expectations for each trigger type.
options.D: A rule that all outputs exceeding 500 words automatically trigger senior review.
options.E: A requirement that reviewers document in writing why they chose NOT to escalate each output.

items.question: An operations director at a manufacturing firm is approving a golden set for evaluating Claude's equipment-maintenance summaries before a department-wide rollout. Which TWO characteristics MOST determine whether the golden set will be an effective benchmark? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The golden set should include only outputs that scored highest in the prior quality review cycle.
options.B: The golden set should include cases from across the full difficulty and complexity range of real maintenance summaries.
options.C: The golden set should be large enough that Claude will not have encountered any of its items in training.
options.D: The golden set's ground truth must be correct and reflect current maintenance standards, not superseded procedures.
options.E: The golden set should be generated by the highest-tier model to ensure the reference outputs are maximally accurate.

items.question: A communications lead at a 90,000-person telecoms company reviews a Claude-drafted internal change-management communication. Review identifies three problems: (1) three factual errors about the change programme timeline, (2) tone appropriate for a press release rather than an internal employee communication, and (3) one section uses language a DEI reviewer flags as stereotyping a demographic group. The communication is due for distribution in 4 hours. Which THREE actions should she take BEFORE deciding whether to regenerate or edit? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Verify the three factual errors against the source programme documentation.
options.B: Assess whether the combination and severity of errors makes regeneration more efficient than editing.
options.C: Route the DEI language concern to the appropriate internal reviewer for a judgment call.
options.D: Publish the communication with a correction notice appended to save time before the deadline.
options.E: Ask Claude to self-evaluate all three issues and propose corrections in a single follow-up prompt.

items.question: A talent acquisition coordinator at a mid-size insurance company uses Claude for four tasks: (1) writing job descriptions for actuarial roles, (2) summarising insurance product FAQs for the company website, (3) drafting performance improvement plan templates for line managers, and (4) generating technical model documentation for internal actuarial systems. Which TWO tasks MOST clearly require a bias review as a distinct quality check? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Tasks 2 and 4, because public-facing and technical content carry the highest reputational risk.
options.B: Task 1, because job descriptions directly influence who applies and may encode exclusionary language.
options.C: Task 4 only, because technical documentation can encode assumptions about the demographics of model users.
options.D: Task 3, because performance improvement plan templates directly affect employment decisions and must not encode differential standards.
options.E: Tasks 1 and 4, because regulated industries require bias review on all AI-generated content.

items.question:
A legal operations manager's team uses Claude to generate contract clause summaries for a new workflow. The pre-defined acceptance threshold is a maximum 10% rejection rate. The first batch of 40 summaries is reviewed against the rubric and 9 (22.5%) fail — significantly above the threshold. The rubric and prompt have been in place for two months. No prompt changes have been made recently.

What should the manager do FIRST?

options.A: Analyse the 9 failures to determine whether they share a common pattern — same clause type, same contract format, or same failure mode — before changing anything.
options.B: Tighten the prompt immediately and resubmit the full batch of 40 summaries for re-review.
options.C: Raise the error-tolerance threshold from 10% to 25% to accommodate this batch's failure rate.
options.D: Escalate immediately to IT to investigate whether a model change has caused the quality degradation.

items.question:
An advertising creative director introduced a quality rubric six months ago requiring that every Claude-generated copy output contain at least three brand-voice markers. Over time, the team began accepting outputs with one or two markers as 'close enough.' Last month, the rubric was formally updated to read: 'sufficient brand-voice markers.' Output quality has visibly declined.

What process failure does this sequence of events illustrate?

options.A: The rubric was too strict to be sustainable, making relaxation inevitable and appropriate.
options.B: The threshold drifted downward informally before being formalised, decoupling the standard from the original business requirement.
options.C: The rubric was amended without IT approval, making it invalid as a quality control document.
options.D: The brand-voice requirement should have been enforced by a prompt constraint rather than a review rubric.

items.question:
An investment compliance officer manages a 16-person team reviewing Claude-generated regulatory summaries. In month 1, the team's pass rate was 78%. By month 6, with no prompt changes and no rubric updates, the pass rate has risen to 94%. The compliance officer is reviewing whether the improvement represents genuine quality gains.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the rising pass rate?

options.A: Reviewers have progressively relaxed their rubric interpretation, raising the effective acceptance threshold without a documented change.
options.B: The underlying model was updated during this period, genuinely improving output quality for regulatory summaries.
options.C: The compliance workload decreased, giving reviewers more time per output and thus finding more acceptable outputs.
options.D: The rubric was calibrated too strictly at launch; the team has now reached the correct operating pass rate.

items.question:
An academic librarian uses Claude to generate a research-topic guide listing all major databases covering a specific subject area. The output is well-organised and reads comprehensively. A subject specialist colleague reviews it and identifies three significant databases that are missing. The librarian accepted the original output without flagging any gaps.

What specific quality check would have caught the omissions the specialist found?

options.A: Source cross-reference — verifying each database listed against a primary index.
options.B: Bias review — checking that the database selection is not skewed toward certain publishers.
options.C: Completeness mapping — comparing the output against a pre-compiled authoritative list of databases in the subject area.
options.D: Golden-set comparison — comparing the topic guide against a previously produced guide in the same subject area.

items.question:
A pharmacy technician at a hospital reviews a Claude-generated drug interaction summary for a high-alert medication. The summary reads coherently and is well-structured. The technician accepts it without verifying that all contraindications listed match the current formulary database. A nurse later identifies a missing contraindication for a common co-medication.

What quality signal should have triggered escalation before acceptance?

options.A: The summary's word count exceeded the expected length for a standard interaction summary.
options.B: The output used hedging language such as 'may interact' rather than definitive statements.
options.C: The drug name appeared in both the header and the body of the summary.
options.D: High-alert medication status combined with the inability to independently verify all listed interactions against a formulary source.

items.question:
A claims adjustment manager at a regional insurer reviews quality audit data across 12 weeks of Claude-output reviews. Error detection rates are consistently 18–22% higher in the first 20 items of each 60-item batch than in items 40–60. The model and prompt have not changed. Each batch takes approximately 3 hours to complete.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the detection-rate gradient?

options.A: Reviewer fatigue causes detection rates to decline progressively through a long batch.
options.B: Earlier items in each batch are systematically less complex than later ones.
options.C: The model produces progressively lower quality output for claims processed later in a batch.
options.D: Reviewers apply stricter standards initially and relax them as they gain confidence in the workflow.

items.question:
An HR data analyst at a technology company has assembled a bias review panel for Claude-generated performance assessment templates. All five panel members are senior managers from the same demographic group — white men aged 45–58. The panel reviews all templates against a standard bias checklist and passes them. Employee groups later raise concerns about differential language in the approved templates.

What quality risk does the panel's composition create?

options.A: The panel may not follow the bias checklist consistently without demographic diversity.
options.B: Language that reads as exclusionary or demeaning to underrepresented groups may be invisible to a panel that has not experienced it as such.
options.C: The panel's authority to approve DEI-sensitive content will be questioned regardless of the quality of their review.
options.D: Without diversity, the panel cannot apply a bias rubric reliably.

items.question:
A biotech regulatory submissions coordinator has used a 20-item golden set for six months to benchmark Claude's protocol summaries. A senior scientist reviewing the golden set discovers that one case has an incorrect expected output — the reference summary cites the wrong regulatory pathway. Claude's outputs consistently 'fail' this case, flagging it as below benchmark.

What does the discovery of this error mean for the benchmark results to date?

options.A: Claude has a confirmed weakness in this case type that must be addressed by prompt engineering.
options.B: The entire golden set is invalidated and must be rebuilt from scratch.
options.C: Claude's 'failures' on this case may not be failures at all — the benchmark must be corrected before the result is interpreted as a model deficiency.
options.D: The benchmark score should be adjusted by removing this case and recalculating without further investigation.

items.question:
An EdTech product manager defines acceptance criteria for Claude-generated quiz questions based on the most common question format: single-answer multiple-choice with one correct option. Claude performs well on these. Three months into production, teachers report that Claude handles multi-part and open-ended questions — which make up 20% of the question bank — poorly.

What failure mode in criteria design does this illustrate?

options.A: The criteria were not reviewed by a subject-matter expert before deployment.
options.B: The criteria used vague language that reviewers interpreted inconsistently.
options.C: The criteria were defined before seeing Claude output, creating a misaligned standard.
options.D: The criteria were designed around the typical case only and do not cover edge-case question types that represent real production risk.

items.question:
A retail operations manager notices that her team consistently accepts any Claude-generated inventory exception report that 'doesn't have obvious errors.' No formal acceptance criteria exist. After six months, managers who use the reports report that they are adequate but never particularly helpful — the reports flag the right issues but never provide the actionable context that would make them decision-ready.

What quality process problem does this describe?

options.A: Without defined criteria, the team is using the absence of obvious errors as an informal quality floor — but 'no obvious errors' may be far below what the use case requires.
options.B: The model needs to be upgraded to produce decision-ready outputs for inventory exception reporting.
options.C: Output volume should be reduced to allow for more careful per-report review.
options.D: Individual reviewer judgment is adequate when outputs consistently appear error-free.

items.question:
A tax consultant at a global firm applies Claude to draft client communications. The firm has two documented quality standards: (1) regulatory standard — all tax positions must cite the specific code sections and rulings that support them; (2) client communication standard — no technical jargon or code references in client-facing letters. An output that fully satisfies standard 1 fails standard 2, and vice versa.

What is the MOST appropriate resolution?

options.A: The regulatory standard always takes precedence; client letters should include code citations even if clients find them hard to follow.
options.B: A structural approach — such as appendixed or footnoted citations — can satisfy both standards without compromising either.
options.C: The client communication standard takes precedence; regulatory citations can be maintained in the internal file rather than the client letter.
options.D: An output that fails either standard must be rejected and regenerated until it satisfies both simultaneously in the same prose.

items.question:
A municipal government analyst implements Claude for drafting public consultation summaries. The escalation policy states: 'Escalate to the department director when uncertain about output quality.' Within four weeks, the director is receiving 30–40 outputs per day for review, has become a bottleneck, and is no longer able to provide timely feedback. Consultation timelines are slipping.

What is the PRIMARY design flaw in the escalation policy?

options.A: The escalation policy does not specify a response-time requirement for the director.
options.B: Reviewers are insufficiently trained to make quality judgments without escalating.
options.C: The escalation trigger ('when uncertain') is too vague to distinguish routine uncertainty from genuine quality-risk signals.
options.D: The director is too senior to be the escalation recipient for routine quality questions.

items.question:
A supply chain analyst uses Claude to transform a 200-line inventory discrepancy table into a formatted exception report. She suspects some rows may have been dropped during the transformation. The output contains 196 line items.

What is the BEST method to verify whether the transformation is complete?

options.A: Review the formatted report for internal consistency — dropped rows would likely create visible formatting gaps.
options.B: Ask Claude to confirm the item count at the end of the report in a follow-up prompt.
options.C: Spot-check 20 random items from the source table to verify they appear in the output.
options.D: Count items in the source table, compare to the output count, then identify the 4 missing rows by matching specific items against the source.

items.question:
A non-profit audit manager uses Claude to generate internal audit summaries. The quality rubric was written for the organisation's legacy report format: structured narrative with section headers. Four months ago, the organisation adopted a new tabular format for audit summaries. The prompt was updated to request tabular outputs. Tabular outputs now consistently fail the rubric, even though the audit director considers them high-quality and prefers the new format.

What quality process failure does this describe?

options.A: The rubric was not updated when the report format changed, so it now tests against requirements that no longer apply.
options.B: Claude changed its output format without authorisation, causing rubric failures.
options.C: The audit director's preference for the new format is a personal opinion that cannot override documented rubric criteria.
options.D: The tabular format produces lower quality than narrative, which is why the rubric rejects it.

items.question:
A media production coordinator uses Claude to compile all broadcast deadlines for the next quarter from a master production calendar. The output lists 14 deadlines. On review, the surrounding context looks correct and the list appears comprehensive, but one deadline shows 14 February when the master calendar specifies 17 February — both dates are Tuesdays in the same month.

What review technique is specifically designed to detect this type of error?

options.A: Completeness mapping — checking that all expected deadlines are present.
options.B: Source cross-reference — verifying each extracted date against the master production calendar.
options.C: Bias review — checking that deadlines are not clustered around particular team members' workloads.
options.D: Acceptance-criteria review — confirming the output meets formatting and count requirements.

items.question:
An energy policy researcher's golden set was built from 20 dense, 800-word analytical summaries written by a departing senior analyst. Claude generates concise, 250-word, bulleted summaries that policymakers describe as 'much more useful for quick briefings.' All Claude outputs fail the golden-set benchmark because they score below the reference outputs on length and density. The policymakers — the actual end users — prefer Claude's format.

What type of golden-set problem is this?

options.A: The golden set is too small to support statistically reliable quality comparisons.
options.B: The ground truth is factually incorrect in the reference summaries.
options.C: The ground truth encodes a style preference of the original author rather than the quality standard of the actual use case, penalising outputs that better serve end users.
options.D: Claude cannot produce summaries that meet the analytical depth required for policy research.

items.question: A financial services firm's compliance team has been running a Claude-assisted regulatory briefing workflow for eight months. Output quality was rated highly in month 1 but has declined progressively despite no prompt changes. A quality audit is commissioned. Which TWO factors MOST commonly cause gradual quality degradation in a long-running Claude workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Reviewers progressively relax their rubric interpretation without documenting the change, effectively lowering the acceptance threshold.
options.B: Claude's model weights decay over time, reducing output quality in long-running deployments.
options.C: The use case or its requirements evolve, but the prompt and acceptance criteria are not updated to match.
options.D: Output volume increases past the point where the model can maintain consistent quality.
options.E: Reviewers gain domain expertise and apply increasingly strict standards, which creates the appearance of declining quality.

items.question: A quality team discovers that one item in their 15-item golden set has an incorrect expected output — the reference summary cites a superseded methodology. The item has been part of the benchmark for eight months. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Remove the item immediately and recalculate the benchmark score without any further investigation.
options.B: Audit the remaining 14 golden-set items for similar errors before declaring the benchmark valid.
options.C: Rebuild the entire golden set from scratch, since one error invalidates all benchmark results.
options.D: Correct the expected output for the affected item through expert review and recalculate the benchmark score.
options.E: Lower the benchmark acceptance threshold to account for the discovered error.

items.question: A quality assurance team is debating whether to patch their existing Claude-output rubric with amendments or rebuild it from scratch. Which THREE conditions MOST clearly indicate that a full rebuild is warranted rather than incremental patching? (Choose THREE)

options.A: The use case has fundamentally changed — the original criteria no longer reflect what the output must accomplish.
options.B: Reviewers consistently interpret criteria differently despite repeated calibration sessions, suggesting structural ambiguity in the criteria language itself.
options.C: The batch pass rate has declined from 82% to 74% over two months.
options.D: New compliance requirements introduce a wholly new quality dimension not addressed anywhere in the existing rubric.
options.E: The model tier used to generate outputs has been changed since the rubric was written.

items.question: A healthcare administrator implements an escalation policy for Claude outputs used in patient-pathway documentation. The policy specifies three escalation triggers clearly but provides no routing information — it does not name recipients or define response timelines. Which TWO consequences are MOST likely? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Reviewers will begin creating informal rubric criteria to replace the escalation triggers.
options.B: Reviewers will stop escalating entirely, since the absence of routing creates too much ambiguity to act.
options.C: Escalation becomes ad hoc, with different reviewers routing to different people based on familiarity rather than expertise.
options.D: Response times become unpredictable, creating delays in patient-pathway documentation when escalated issues go unresolved.
options.E: The escalation policy will be formally replaced by a spot-check process within three months.

items.question:
A legal operations coordinator notices that a 6-month-old rubric for Claude-generated contract summaries consistently rejects outputs that the requesting attorneys consider high-quality and useful. The rubric's formatting requirements were derived from a style guide revised 4 months ago. Attorneys have not raised formal quality concerns. The coordinator suspects the rubric no longer reflects current standards.

What should the coordinator do NEXT?

options.A: Accept all attorney-approved outputs regardless of rubric result and document each exception individually.
options.B: Compare the rubric's current criteria against the revised style guide to identify specifically which criteria are now outdated.
options.C: Raise the rubric's error-tolerance threshold to reduce the pass rate to attorney-approval rate.
options.D: Instruct Claude to generate summaries in the format specified by the original style guide until the rubric is formally updated.

items.question:
A general counsel at a 90-person law firm wants to implement Claude for two tasks: (1) drafting client advisories on regulatory changes that will be distributed to clients, and (2) drafting internal meeting agenda items. She asks her operations manager how acceptance criteria should differ between the two tasks.

What is the MOST appropriate guidance?

options.A: Define separate acceptance criteria for each use case, calibrated to the consequences of an error — stricter for client advisories, lighter for internal agendas.
options.B: Define a single high standard for all outputs, since any Claude output could unexpectedly be shared externally.
options.C: Define criteria only for the client advisories; internal agendas require minimal review and do not warrant documented criteria.
options.D: Apply identical criteria to both tasks to prevent reviewers from accidentally applying the wrong standard to the wrong output.

items.question:
An HR director at a global fintech company has reviewed Claude-generated candidate assessment summaries for three months. A bias audit reveals that across 300 assessments, female candidates are systematically described using support-oriented language ('keen to collaborate,' 'supportive of team goals') while male candidates receive strategic language ('decisive,' 'results-oriented'). The HR director has been editing individual summaries to correct the language before use.

What should the HR director recommend going forward?

options.A: Continue editing individual summaries — the current approach corrects each assessment before it is used.
options.B: Reject the current prompt and restart with explicit bias-prevention instructions, since systematic language bias requires a prompt-level fix rather than output-level editing.
options.C: Escalate the pattern to the model vendor as a product defect requiring a fix.
options.D: Implement a stricter acceptance threshold that requires language parity checks on every output before acceptance.

items.question:
A diversity lead at a non-profit advocacy organisation uses Claude to generate job descriptions for 10 open roles. On review, 7 of 10 descriptions use the phrase 'strong hacker mentality' and 'fast-paced ninja team.' These phrases were not in the brief. The diversity lead knows this terminology is associated with deterring non-male applicants.

What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Edit each of the 7 descriptions to remove the problematic phrases.
options.B: Accept the descriptions — 'hacker' and 'ninja' are common in non-profit tech culture and are unlikely to deter qualified applicants.
options.C: Reject and restart with explicit prompt instructions prohibiting male-coded technical jargon and specifying inclusive language requirements.
options.D: Accept the 3 descriptions without the phrases and escalate the 7 to HR leadership before deciding.

items.question:
A communications director at a financial services firm reviews a Claude-drafted shareholder letter. The facts are accurate, all required sections are present, the legal disclosures are complete, but the tone is 'friendly and conversational' where the firm's investor communications standard requires 'formal and institutional.' No structural or factual issues exist.

What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.A: Reject and restart — tone failures in shareholder communications require a full restart.
options.B: Escalate to the investor relations team for approval before making any changes.
options.C: Accept the letter — minor tone variations do not affect the legal validity of the communication.
options.D: Edit the draft to adjust tone and register — the structure and content are correct, making this edit-appropriate.

items.question:
A QA manager at a healthcare IT company proposes the following process: run Claude on 200 data-extraction tasks, identify the top-quality outputs by expert review, use those outputs as the golden set, and then derive acceptance criteria from the characteristics of the golden set. She argues this ensures criteria are achievable and grounded in real outputs.

What is the FUNDAMENTAL flaw in this approach?

options.A: Deriving acceptance criteria from the model's best outputs anchors the standard to what Claude can produce rather than to what the use case requires, creating circular validation.
options.B: The golden set should be built before the prompt is finalised, not after running outputs.
options.C: Acceptance criteria must be approved by a compliance officer before a golden set can be built.
options.D: Expert review is not a reliable method for identifying high-quality outputs to use as golden-set references.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs manager at a pharmaceutical company uses Claude to generate summaries of clinical study reports for FDA submission. Reviewing a batch of 40 summaries, she finds that 6 omit the 'adverse events' section. In the same workflow used for internal research reviews, she previously accepted a 15% omission rate as tolerable. The current batch is destined for an FDA submission package.

How should she apply the completeness threshold for this context?

options.A: Apply the same 15% internal tolerance — adverse events are addressed in a separate section of the FDA package.
options.B: Apply near-zero tolerance — adverse event omissions in an FDA submission carry patient safety and regulatory non-compliance consequences that make completeness non-negotiable.
options.C: Accept the batch and note the 6 omissions as exceptions in the submission cover letter.
options.D: The completeness threshold is set by the FDA reviewer, not the internal team.

items.question:
An L&D manager at a large retailer has an acceptance rubric for Claude-generated training materials covering accuracy, completeness, and tone. A colleague in the DEI team points out that training materials shape workplace culture and expectations, and that the rubric has no bias criterion. The colleague suggests adding one.

What is the BEST form for a bias criterion in this rubric?

options.A: A requirement that Claude generate materials from a perspective-neutral standpoint.
options.B: A criterion requiring legal review of all training content for employment law compliance before acceptance.
options.C: A criterion specifying review against a documented list of exclusionary terms and a diverse reviewer panel assessment before materials are accepted for distribution.
options.D: A criterion requiring that materials be piloted with a representative employee group before final acceptance.

items.question:
A brand manager at an advertising agency is building a golden set to benchmark Claude's brand copy for a retail client. All 15 reference outputs in the golden set are from 18 months ago, when the brand used long-form narrative prose. The client recently refreshed the brand to short, punchy, headline-driven copy. The brand manager uses the existing golden set as the benchmark.

What is the PRIMARY risk in this approach?

options.A: The golden set is too small to reliably benchmark brand copy quality.
options.B: Long-form and short-form prose cannot be compared using the same quality criteria.
options.C: The agency should obtain client approval before using any golden-set reference outputs.
options.D: The golden set encodes the old brand style, making it invalid as a benchmark for current brand compliance.

items.question:
A content lead at a media start-up runs 50 blog posts through Claude without pre-defining acceptance criteria. Three posts are clearly off-topic (different industry). The remaining 47 are roughly on-topic but vary in depth, structure, and quality. She is unsure which of the 47 are good enough. Her editor asks her to explain her quality-assurance challenge.

What is the PRIMARY problem she faces?

options.A: Without pre-defined acceptance criteria, she cannot distinguish genuinely good-enough outputs from borderline cases — every ambiguous decision requires ad hoc judgment with no consistent standard.
options.B: She should reject all 50 and restart with a more constrained prompt.
options.C: The three off-topic posts indicate the model is fundamentally unreliable for blog content generation.
options.D: She should upgrade to a higher-tier model before defining criteria.

items.question:
A senior partner at a mid-size law firm reviews escalation data for Claude-generated contract summaries. An associate escalates 100% of outputs with the justification 'I'm always uncertain about legal accuracy.' The partner asks the associate to develop a principle for distinguishing escalation-warranting uncertainty from routine uncertainty.

What principle BEST distinguishes these two types of uncertainty?

options.A: Escalation-warranting uncertainty is determined by output length — longer outputs carry more uncertainty and should be escalated.
options.B: Escalation-warranting uncertainty is grounded in a specific, observable quality signal — an unverifiable claim, a factual contradiction, or a required element that cannot be verified — not in a general sense that something might be wrong.
options.C: All legal outputs carry sufficient uncertainty to warrant escalation — 100% escalation is appropriate for legal content.
options.D: Escalation-warranting uncertainty occurs only when the output has been reviewed by two people who disagree.

items.question:
A product marketing manager at a SaaS company reviews Claude-generated product launch emails. The outputs use the correct brand voice and tone throughout. On a second pass, she notices that 4 of 12 emails omit the mandatory competitive comparison table required by the product launch brief.

What should the review flag, and what does it illustrate about multi-dimensional quality review?

options.A: A tone failure — the emails lack the detail-oriented formality expected in a product launch.
options.B: An escalation trigger — missing tables may indicate the model is generating from incomplete context.
options.C: A completeness failure; brand voice compliance and completeness against the brief are independent dimensions, and passing one does not guarantee passing the other.
options.D: A rubric gap — the rubric should have specified the comparison table as a required element.

items.question:
A talent analytics manager at an enterprise tech firm applies a 'good enough' threshold for Claude-generated job descriptions: 'accurate and professionally written.' All descriptions pass this threshold. A bias audit six months later finds that descriptions for senior roles (predominantly held by men) consistently use achievement language, while descriptions for support roles (predominantly held by women) use collaboration language — a pattern that can reinforce occupational segregation.

What does this scenario demonstrate?

options.A: The 'accurate and professionally written' threshold is too vague to be useful as an acceptance criterion.
options.B: Bias audits should replace standard acceptance criteria in recruitment content.
options.C: The threshold successfully identified the bias through the accuracy criterion.
options.D: A 'good enough' threshold that omits bias review allows outputs to meet defined criteria while embedding systematic bias.

items.question:
A solo financial planner defines acceptance criteria for Claude-generated client financial summaries. One criterion states: 'Every figure in the output must be traceable to the source data provided.' Reviewing a summary, she finds that a projected return figure of 8.7% does not appear in or derive from any of the source documents she provided.

What does this finding represent?

options.A: The acceptance criterion has been violated; the untraceable figure is a clear quality failure and escalation trigger under her own criteria.
options.B: The figure may be correct even if not in the source data — Claude may have calculated it from available inputs.
options.C: This is a formatting failure — the source citation was not included in the output.
options.D: The criterion was too strict; a good projected return figure can be independently reasonable without appearing in source data.

items.question:
A talent acquisition lead at a professional services firm has spent three months editing individual Claude-generated candidate assessments to remove gendered language. Each batch of 40 assessments requires approximately 15 edits to correct. The pattern persists identically in every new batch despite the editing work. The lead's manager asks her to recommend a sustainable approach.

What should the talent lead recommend?

options.A: Increase the editing team size so that 15 edits per batch can be completed faster.
options.B: Reject the current prompt and restart with explicit inclusive-language requirements, addressing systematic bias at the source rather than output by output.
options.C: Escalate to the model provider to investigate why the bias pattern is persistent.
options.D: Reduce batch size so each batch requires fewer total edits per cycle.

items.question:
The head of communications at an energy company reviews a Claude-drafted press release. The draft: (1) uses correct brand voice throughout, (2) contains accurate and complete product information, (3) is missing the two-sentence mandatory 'About the Company' boilerplate required in all press releases. The boilerplate is templated and takes 30 seconds to add.

Should the head of communications edit the draft or reject and restart?

options.A: Reject and restart — any completeness failure in a public communication requires full regeneration.
options.B: Escalate to the PR director before deciding — missing boilerplate may signal other missing elements.
options.C: Edit — the structure, brand voice, and content are all correct; inserting a templated two-sentence boilerplate is targeted editing, not a structural fix.
options.D: Accept — 'About the Company' boilerplate is optional in time-sensitive press releases.

items.question: A financial analyst at an investment bank is designing the acceptance conditions for Claude-generated due diligence summaries that will be shared with acquisition deal teams. The summaries must be ready for distribution without further senior review. Which TWO conditions must BOTH be satisfied for a summary to be accepted without escalation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: All required sections from the due diligence checklist are present and substantively addressed.
options.B: The summary was generated using the same model tier as the golden-set reference outputs.
options.C: The summary has received at least two independent review cycles from the same reviewer.
options.D: Every material claim and figure in the summary is verifiable against the source documents provided.
options.E: The summary is formatted identically to the golden-set reference outputs.

items.question: An HR director at a large enterprise is designing a quality gate for Claude-generated promotion committee materials — assessments and supporting documents that will inform decisions on 150 candidates. Which TWO quality dimensions MOST require both a stricter-than-standard acceptance threshold AND a specific review technique beyond a general read-through? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Output formatting and visual consistency across documents.
options.B: Demographic bias in descriptive language about candidates.
options.C: Completeness against the promotion criteria brief — ensuring all required evaluation dimensions are addressed for each candidate.
options.D: File naming conventions and metadata compliance.

items.question: A risk manager at a wealth management firm reviews a Claude-generated client risk profile due for distribution in 2 hours. The review identifies: (1) client assets are understated by 15% — a likely extraction error, (2) a mandatory regulatory disclosure section is absent, and (3) risk categorisation language treats clients from two geographic regions differently. Which THREE actions should she take BEFORE deciding whether to edit or restart? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Verify the asset figure against the client's account data to confirm the error and determine its magnitude.
options.B: Determine whether the regulatory disclosure section is legally required for this client type and jurisdiction.
options.C: Route the geography-based language differential to the compliance team for a ruling on whether it constitutes biased treatment.
options.D: Regenerate the entire report with a corrected prompt immediately to meet the 2-hour deadline.
options.E: Distribute the report with a verbal disclaimer to the client explaining the known issues.
